zh.summary: 为开发者与 AI 编程代理提供更快的构建、测试和运行基础设施。
zh.judgment: 生成代码越便宜，验证与执行越可能成为瓶颈；商业价值要用可靠交付与真实计算成本证明。
zh.replaces: 团队自建或维护构建机器、处理缓存和等待测试队列。
zh.segment: 开发与 AI 代理基础设施
zh.product: 官网展示构建与持续集成加速，融资档案将其定位为 AI 编程代理的基础层。它不负责判断代码需求是否正确；研究应区分“执行更快”和“最终发布的软件更可靠”两种结果。
zh.customer: 使用者是开发团队和平台工程人员，预算承担者可能是工程组织，此为商业推断。代理生成更多代码后可能放大测试、构建与隔离环境需求，但这个因果假设需要真实运行量和付费合同支持，不能由 AI 热度直接推出。
zh.workflow: 合理的工作链是接入现有项目、执行构建与测试、利用缓存降低重复工作，再将结果送回开发流程。官网提供相关能力展示；进一步尽调应测试冷启动、失败重试、并发峰值与日志可追溯性，而非只比较最佳缓存命中场景。
zh.business_model: 已核验价目：Developer 按用量付费，Team 每月 100 美元、Business 250 美元，各带计算分钟和构建额度，Enterprise 询价。不同资源与超额用量会改变实际费用；机器利用率、缓存及峰值预留影响毛利。
zh.traction: 官网有客户案例与速度提升声明，属于公司发布的个案，不是所有项目的普遍结果。仍缺付费客户留存、跨语言项目的性能分布与净成本对照，因此不能从一个加速案例直接推出高增长或高利润。
zh.moat: 云服务、既有持续集成供应商与团队自建工具都构成替代。潜在壁垒是稳定执行、缓存技术和开发流程集成；模型本身不是这里的主要护城河。若迁移成本低，性价比与可靠性将持续受到比较。
zh.funding_read: B 轮相较种子前项目更偏向规模执行，但轮次并不替代收入或留存证据。下一商业里程碑可看大客户扩用与高峰容量下的盈利能力；具体资金分配和估值未在本次证据中确认。
zh.risks: 硬件与算力成本可能吞掉表面增长，依赖单一生态也可能受到原生平台竞争。代理产生更多低价值测试，还可能放大使用量却不提升客户效果，需要把运行量与有效交付分开衡量。
zh.takeaway: 可借鉴在生成能力扩张后寻找后续瓶颈：验证、隔离、运行与回滚往往比再加一个生成入口更有采购理由。产品设计应把速度、稳定性和总成本同时呈现，方便客户做真实迁移判断。
zh.watch_next: 看成功测试与构建的单次成本、缓存命中率、失败恢复、客户扩用和容量毛利。若实际工作负载中总成本下降、稳定性不下降且客户续费，才有更强的商业证据。

en.summary: Build, test and execution infrastructure for developers and AI coding agents.
en.judgment: As generation gets cheaper, verification can become the bottleneck; reliable delivery and compute economics must prove the value.
en.replaces: Maintaining build machines, managing caches and waiting for test queues.
en.product: The site presents build and CI acceleration; the funding profile frames an agent infrastructure opportunity. Faster execution and more reliable final software are separate outcomes and should be evaluated separately.
en.customer: Developers and platform teams are users, with engineering organisations as plausible buyers. More agent-produced code may increase verification demand, but actual paid workload must substantiate this hypothesis.
en.workflow: Integration, builds, tests, caching and returned results form the evaluation chain. Cold starts, retries, concurrency and traceable logs should be tested alongside favourable cache-hit benchmarks.
en.business_model: The reviewed page lists usage-based Developer, Team at $100/month and Business at $250 with compute/build allowances, and custom Enterprise. Resources and overages change actual bills; utilization, caching and peak reserves affect margin.
en.traction: Company-published customer cases and speed claims do not represent all workloads. Retention, performance distributions and comparable total costs remain important missing evidence.
en.moat: Cloud services, CI vendors and internal tooling provide substitutes. Stable execution, caching and workflow integration are potential strengths. Low migration cost would leave price and reliability under continued comparison.
en.funding_read: Series B implies a different funding stage from pre-seed, but does not establish revenue or retention. Account expansion and profitable peak capacity would be useful milestones. Valuation and allocation were not confirmed.
en.risks: Compute costs could absorb growth; ecosystem dependence creates incumbent competition. More low-value agent tests could raise usage without improving customer outcomes, so activity and useful delivery must be separated.
en.takeaway: Look for the bottleneck after generation expands: verification, isolation, execution and recovery can have clear procurement value. Show speed, reliability and total cost together to support a meaningful migration decision.
en.watch_next: Watch cost per successful build or test, cache hits, recovery, customer expansion and capacity margins. Lower total cost without lost reliability, followed by renewals, would be stronger commercial evidence.

Contact us . Compute What are unit minutes? Namespace accounts usage based on "compute units". A compute unit represents using 1 vCPU and 2GB of RAM for a minute times the platform multiplier (i.e. 1 for Linux). How are unit minutes calculated? For Linux, if you run an instance that has 4 vCPU and 8GB RAM for 5 minutes, then that's: 4 (vCPU) x 5 (minutes) x 1 (Linux multiplier) = 20 unit minutes For Windows, running an instance with 2 vCPU and 4GB RAM for 6 minutes is: 2 (vCPU) x 6 (minutes) x 2 (Windows multiplier) = 24 unit minutes For Mac, an instance with 6 vCPU and 14GB RAM running for 3 minutes is: 6 (vCPU) x 3 (minutes) x 10 (Mac multiplier) = 180 unit minutes While we account for a minimum of 1 minute, we always round the next 15 seconds down. For example, 30 seconds of usage is 1 billable minute, 70 seconds is 1 billable minute, and 150 seconds are billed as 3 minutes. Unit minutes usage per shape can be found under " What is the unit minutes usage and price for each shape? " below . What is a standard shape? For Linux and Windows, our standard shapes are multiples of 1 vCPU and 2GB RAM. For shapes with a different ratio (i.e., 1 vCPU, 4GB RAM), compute units are calculated as: max(vCPU count, GB RAM divided by 2) For example, running a Linux instance on 8 vCPU and 32GB RAM for 2 minutes will be: 16 (32GB RAM / 2) x 2 (minutes) x 1 (Linux multiplier) = 32 unit minutes Unit minutes usage per shape can be found under " What is the unit minutes usage and price for each shape? " below . How are Linux, Windows and macOS priced? Jobs that run on Windows or macOS consume minutes at a higher rate than jobs on Linux, they consume 2x and 10x the rate respectively. compute and storage. Reuse action results across CI, local, and Devbox builds, and
run the actions themselves on workers that Namespace keeps running, so a build does
not wait for capacity to come up. ​ Getting Started 1 Configure access Generate a bazelrc that points Bazel at Namespace. Start with the cache, and add
remote execution when you want the actions to run on Namespace compute too. Cache only Remote Execution nsc bazel setup --remote=false --bazelrc= ~ /.namespace.bazelrc This command provisions a remote Bazel cache, if needed, and writes a bazelrc with the relevant configuration options. nsc bazel setup --bazelrc= ~ /.namespace.bazelrc This command provisions the execution cluster if needed, and writes a bazelrc with the remote executor, remote cache, and credentials. 2 Run Bazel bazel --bazelrc= ~ /.namespace.bazelrc build //... You can pass multiple --bazelrc flags if you need to combine Namespace’s generated
configuration with your existing project configuration. Bazel reads the files in the
order it is given them, and where two files set the same option, the last one read
wins. See bazelrc files for the full order, which
also covers the workspace and home rc files Bazel picks up on its own. ​ Caching and Remote Execution The Bazel cache shares action results across invocations and
machines. It applies to any action Bazel can cache, and the saving is largest where
compilation is slow, such as Rust and C++ codebases. The cache is shared, so CI and
local builds reuse each other’s results. Remote Execution runs the actions themselves on Namespace
compute, scaling a build across many workers for high parallelism. Its workers keep
low-latency access to the cache, so remotely executed actions read and write the
same artifacts as everything else. Actions can also be routed to workers on a
different platform than the machine running Bazel, which is how a Linux host can
drive a macOS build. ​ Common setups Bazel cache from GitHub Actions Turn on Bazel caching in your Namespace runner profile. Your workflow needs no changes. Cross-platform builds Drive a macOS or iOS build from a Linux host by routing actions to macOS workers. GitHub Actions on GitHub-hosted runners Reach the Namespace cache from GitHub’s own runners, to try it before moving your runners. Bazel from a Devbox Enable Bazel caching when creating a Devbox, and builds use it with no further setup.
